<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin="par147" />subject and copula (as Gn 18<sub>9</sub> {{GHGheb|text=הִנֵּה בָאֹ֫הֶל|translate=behold}} she is ''in the tent''; 42:28), or there is no indication whatever of the predicate, so that the sentence is limited to {{GHGheb|text=הִנֵּה}} with the suffix, as in the frequent use of {{GHGheb|text=הִנֵּ֫נִי}}, {{GHGheb|text=הִנֶּ֫נִּי|translate=here am I}}, in answer to an address. Elsewhere a substantive follows {{GHGheb|text=הִנֵּה}} (or {{GHGheb|text=הֵן}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=11|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=31|verse=35}}), and {{GHGheb|text=הִנֵּה}} then includes the meaning of a demonstrative pronoun and the copula, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=22|verse=7}} {{GHGheb|text=הִנֵּה הָאֵשׁ וְהָֽעֵצִים|translate=here is the fire and the wood}}, &c.; 12:19 ''behold'' thou hast ''thy wife!'' {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=24|verse=8}}; with reference to the past, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=7|verse=1}} {{GHGheb|text=וְהִנֵּה לֶ֫קֶשׁ וג׳|translate=and lo}}, it was ''the latter growth'', &c. By a very pregnant construction the simple {{GHGheb|text=הִנֵּה}} is used as the equivalent of a sentence in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=9|verse=19}}, ''lo, here am I!''

{{GHGmargin-letter|147|c}}
'''3.''' Examples of exclamations (threatening, complaining, triumphing, especially warlike or seditious) in which, owing to the excitement of the speaker, some indispensable member of the sentence is suppressed, are—(''a'') with suppression of the predicate (which has frequently to be supplied in the form of a jussive), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=7|verse=20}} ''a sword for the Lord and for Gideon!'' (verse 18 without {{GHGheb|text=חֶ֫רֶב}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=20|verse=1}} and {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=10|verse=16}} (cf. also {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=22|verse=36}}) ''every man to his tents, O Israel!'' (i.e. ''let every man go to'' or ''remain in his tent''); without {{GHGheb|text=אִישׁ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=12|verse=16}}; moreover, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=1|verse=28}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=13|verse=4|hidebook=1}} (on the exclamatory {{GHGheb|text=קוֹל}} equivalent to ''hark!'' cf. {{GHGpar|146|b}}); 28:10, 29:16 ({{GHGheb|text=הַפְכְּכֶם|translate=O your perversity!}} i.e. how great it is!); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=49|verse=16}} (if {{GHGheb|text=תִּפְלַצְתְּךָ}} be equivalent to ''terror be upon thee!''); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jo|chapter=4|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mal|chapter=1|verse=13}} ({{GHGheb|text=הִנֵּה מַתְּלָאָה|translate=behold what a weariness!}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=22|verse=29}}; perhaps also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=49|verse=4}} {{GHGheb|text=פַּ֫חַז כַּמַּ֫יִם|translate=a bubbling over as water}} (sc. happened), unless it is better to supply a subject {{GHGheb|text=אַתָּה}} (''thou wast'').—(''b'') With suppression of the subject, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=4|verse=20}}, cf. {{GHGpar|152|k}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=15|verse=23}} {{GHGheb|text=אַיֵּה|translate=where}} sc. is bread?—(''c'') With suppression of both subject and predicate, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=7|verse=18}} (see above); {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=12|verse=16}} (see above); {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=9|verse=27}} {{GHGheb|text=גַּם אֹתוֹ|translate=him also!}} explained immediately afterwards by {{GHGheb|text=הַכֻּהוּ|translate=smite him!}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=5|verse=8}} ''after thee, Benjamin!'' sc. is the enemy (differently in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=5|verse=14}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=6|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=90|verse=13|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Hb|chapter=2|verse=6}} {{GHGheb|text=עַד־מָתַי}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=74|verse=9}} {{GHGheb|text=עַד־מָה}}.—On {{GHGheb|text=וָלֹא|translate=and if not}} (unless {{GHGheb|text=וְלוּ}} is to be read), {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=13|verse=26}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=5|verse=17}}, see § 158 dd.

{{GHGmargin-letter|147|d}}
Rem. 1. To the class of incomplete sentences naturally belong exclamations introduced by interjections {{GHGheb|text=אֲהָהּ}}, {{GHGheb|text=אוֹי}}, {{GHGheb|text=הוֹי}}, {{GHGheb|text=הַס}};<ref>We do not consider here the cases in which these interjections (e.g. {{GHGheb|text=הַם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=3|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=6|verse=10}}) stand quite disconnectedly (so always {{GHGheb|text=אָח}} and {{GHGheb|text=הֶאָח}}).</ref> cf. § 105. After the first two the object of the ''threat'' or ''imprecation'' follows regularly with {{GHGheb|text=לְ}} (cf. ''vae tibi'') or {{GHGheb|text=אֶל־}} or {{GHGheb|text=עַל־}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אוֹי לָ֫נוּ|translate=woe unto us!}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=4|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=6|verse=5}}; cf. also {{GHGheb|text=אֲהָהּ לַיּוֹם|translate=alas for the day!}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jo|chapter=1|verse=15}}; on the other hand, the object of ''commiseration'' (after {{GHGheb|text=הוֹי}}) follows mostly in the vocative, or rather in the accusative of exclamation (cf. ''vae te'' in Plautus); so in lamentation for the dead, {{GHGheb|text=הוֹי אָחִי|translate=alas, my brother!}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=13|verse=30}},<section end="par147" /><noinclude>
